extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, corporate communications teams, marketing executives
extracted.subtask_description: Practical lessons and checklist items for handling public relations crises, drawn from five high-profile case studies and general crisis-preparation advice. Aimed at helping communications teams avoid pitfalls and prepare written response plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a Global Perspective
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising campaigns are often the root of PR scandals. Note to every advertising team: please bring in your PR team to review your ad campaigns before launch. A diverse group of executives makes a company’s messages stronger — companies need all kinds of voices to share how an ad or PR campaign can be read from perspectives across sex, race, and gender. If something in the room feels 'a little off,' speak up; if you are having a reaction, others likely will too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Sincere Apologies
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apology is not an apology if it’s not delivered in a humble manner that avoids all defensive inclinations. Coach the executive making the apology: bring them into the writing process, explain reasoning for language, coach concise responses, and remind them the goal is sincerity. If the executive won’t cooperate, select another spokesperson. You only get one opportunity to get your response out there, so work tirelessly to get it right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think it Through (consider human impact)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major decisions that affect human lives (employees and consumers) should be taken with greater care, discussion, and thought. Avoid decisions driven solely by time or cost efficiency that show little regard for people's livelihoods. Involve more executive leadership (not just HR) to prevent avoidable insensitive choices and the appearance of prioritizing the bottom line over people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optics Matter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how company or executive actions will look to the public eye — even well-intended communications can appear self-serving. Review statements and accompanying imagery (e.g., a selfie of a crying CEO) through a PR lens and adjust to avoid redirecting sympathy away from affected parties. A simple adjustment (e.g., a statement without a photo) could be better received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit to your Mistakes (quick acknowledgment)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A company almost always benefits from a quick response that admits a mistake. A direct, well-timed response shows people you received their message and are making corrections. Companies with a long history of trust have an even better chance of being forgiven. Quick admission and corrective action are often what the public seeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a Written PR Crisis Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: PR crisis plan prepared in writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best course is to have a PR crisis plan prepared in writing. It should be detailed and include specifics (see related checklist items). Creating the plan should be accompanied by ongoing efforts to build public trust via community engagement, sponsorships, donations, and corporate transparency and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: List Response Team Members
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of the response team members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about who is on the crisis response team so responsibilities are clear during an incident. The plan should identify each member and their role to streamline decision-making and communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coach Executives in Advance of Public Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A plan to quickly coach executives in advance of their public statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a rapid coaching process: craft and explain statement language, rehearse concise answers to likely questions, and ensure the speaker understands tone and humility required. If the executive cannot deliver an appropriate apology or statement, designate a different spokesperson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond Quickly but Vetted
rubrics_metrics.description: A goal to respond quickly, but not so quickly that responses aren’t completely vetted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance speed with accuracy and tone: respond promptly to acknowledge the issue, but ensure messaging is vetted to avoid defensiveness or missteps that amplify the crisis (e.g., defensive CEO statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build Ongoing Public Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing company effort to build trust with the public by being a good community member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice corporate transparency and responsibility, share and make good on company values, give back through sponsorships and donations. This foundation increases the likelihood of surviving fallout from a PR disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Company Statements and Then Move On
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your company statements and then move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus effort on getting the initial response right; once a clear, well-crafted statement is released, avoid dwelling on the matter. Consumers are usually forgiving and ready to move on if the first response is handled properly.
